extracted.intended_audience: independent TV writers/producers (UK) preparing pitches/proposals for Channel 4
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for developing and submitting a programme proposal to Channel 4, including what the broadcaster looks for, the submission/meeting process, budgeting and timetable approvals, marketing considerations, delivery requirements, and example proposal content for a documentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: ITC commissioning quota / independent sector opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The ITC regulations state that at least 25% of a broadcaster's non-current affairs/news output should be commissioned to the independent sector and this gives up and coming writers and directors a chance to get their idea’s onto the silver screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this regulatory requirement to justify independent commissioning eligibility and to frame proposals as opportunities for Channel 4 to meet commissioning quotas; highlights that independents are an intended source of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel 4 commissioning categories & category-specific requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel 4 has a page dedicated to commissioning on its website that anyone can look at. It has 17 categories ranging from Comedy to Online. In each category, Channel 4 outline what they’re looking for in some detail, in that specific category giving you details about what slot it will go in, examples of previously commissioned shows that are similar to what they’re looking for as well as who you should contact concerning your idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before pitching, identify the correct Channel 4 category and read its specific guidance: expected slot, comparable commissions, and named contacts; tailor proposal to the category's stated needs and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Channel 4 looks for in commissioned content
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel 4 are looking for “compelling and arresting British stories” as well as something that is “multi – narrative”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame ideas as compelling, distinctly British and multi-narrative where appropriate; demonstrate distinctiveness and emotional or narrative arresting qualities. Use examples and comparable commissions to show fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal submission and initial commissioning meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have your idea you should send a proposal to the Commissioning Officer and if they like your idea and see potential in it they will up a meeting where you will discuss the idea in more detail, seeing if your idea will work across other departments or platforms. If after all of this they still like your idea you will be awarded the production money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit a clear proposal to the named Commissioning Officer; prepare to present the idea in a meeting, discuss cross-department/platform potential, and demonstrate scalability and departmental fit to secure funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production timetable agreement (who signs off)
rubrics_metrics.description: When your idea has been further developed, the Commissioning Editor, Business Affairs and the Programme Finance Manager will agree on a production timetable which looks at how the budget will be spent in every phase of making the programme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect timetable negotiation among editorial, legal/rights (Business Affairs) and finance; provide realistic phase-by-phase budgets and schedules to facilitate agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget approval stages
rubrics_metrics.description: The budget has to be processed through three stages. Firstly by the Commissioning Editor and the Finance then by the Head of Department. Finally the budget is scrutinised by the Programme Finance Committee. The final agreement is usually signed six weeks before pre-production starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for a three-stage budget review: (1) Commissioning Editor & Finance, (2) Head of Department, (3) Programme Finance Committee. Aim to have final budgets agreed ~6 weeks before pre-production and provide supporting cost detail for each review stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing and press potential
rubrics_metrics.description: When production begins the marketing and press potential of your programme is discussed. This means if what advertising campaigns can be produced to raise awareness of you programme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how the programme can be marketed: potential campaigns, press hooks, and audience-engagement strategies. Prepare marketing angles and promotional assets early to discuss at production start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery and technical/programme delivery requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery of your programme should be made with all technical and programme delivery requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure final delivery meets broadcaster technical specs and programme delivery requirements (formats, metadata, legal clearances); confirm technical checklist early and allow time for compliance before transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-broadcast feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback is then given on your programme after it has been broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan to receive and use post-transmission feedback from the broadcaster; use feedback to inform future commissions or re-development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal content & positioning (example elements from 'My Idea')
rubrics_metrics.description: Example proposal includes: a clear concept (a documentary about two British players in the NFL), demonstration of why the story fits Channel 4 ('compelling and arresting British stories', 'multi – narrative'), proposed slot (10 o’clock weekday), target audience (fans and general viewers seeking heart-warming inspirational stories), narrator choice (Vernon Kay) and ties to Channel 4 programming (NFL broadcasts, Super Bowl coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting a proposal include: narrative summary, why the story fits the category and slot, target audience, proposed presenter/narrator, evidence of audience/timing fit, and any programming tie-ins or topical relevance to Channel 4 line-up. Use personal interviews, archival/material access and clear narrative arcs as selling points.
